preamble: The shift from the voiceless alveolar stop [t] to the voiceless dental fricative [θ] is one of the most widely documented consonant changes in historical phonology. It occurs via two main pathways: spirantization (weakening of a stop to a fricative, often in intervocalic or post-vocalic position) and Grimm's Law-type chain shifts in which an entire class of voiceless stops acquires friction. The change is attested across Germanic and Celtic.

examples.note: Grimm's Law (First Germanic Consonant Shift, c. 500–200 BCE): PIE voiceless stops *p *t *k shifted to fricatives *f *θ *x in Proto-Germanic. The *t → *θ arm is the most visible, preserved as ⟨th⟩ [θ] in Gothic and Old English. Latin tres vs. English three exemplifies the change.
The coda *t → *θ is visible in Gothic ⟨þ⟩ and in the English spelling ⟨th⟩. Compare Latin dens (genitive dentis), which preserves the original stop.
Medial *t gave *þ where the accent preceded it; after an unstressed syllable Verner's law gave *ð instead (*fadēr).
Intervocalic *t became a voiceless dental fricative; Old Irish writes non-initial ⟨th⟩ for [θ] (áth /aːθ/ 'ford'), contrasting with Brythonic voicing to *d (*rrod, *bɨd).

sources: Campbell, L. (2013). Historical Linguistics: An Introduction (3rd ed.). Edinburgh University Press; MIT Press. https://lccn.loc.gov/2012038044

Fortson, B. W. (2010). Indo-European Language and Culture: An Introduction (2nd ed.). Wiley-Blackwell. https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Indo-European+Language+and+Culture%3A+An+Introduction%2C+2nd+Edition-p-9781405188968
